intro: Financial advisors analyze complex situations, build trust and explain money clearly, skills that finance leadership values. The closest of the 25 careers below are Financial Managers and Investment Fund Managers, both at an 88% skill match; financial managers earn a BLS May 2025 median of $166,570, or 59% more than the $105,070 advisors earn.
why_it_works: Advising clients means reading their goals and fears, building plans and keeping them calm when markets drop. O*NET rates complex problem solving, judgment, social perceptiveness and service orientation at 3.62 out of 5 for this job. Finance management, analysis and benefits roles use the same skills. Most matches need no new degree. The gaps are managing people and materials.
tips: Management Analysts earn $101,860 and are an 85% match if you want salaried consulting work.
Compensation and Benefits Managers earn $149,230, which is 42% more, and use your planning skills.
Lead a small team or mentor new advisors; managing people is your most common gap.

faq.q: What jobs can former financial advisors do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Financial Managers (88%), Investment Fund Managers (88%) and financial services sales agents (87%), based on O*NET 31.0. Treasurers and Controllers are also 85% matched, with a median of $166,570 for their broader BLS group.

faq.q: Which careers for financial advisors pay more?
faq.a: 13 of the 25 matches pay more than $105,070. Financial Managers earn $166,570 (59% more), Marketing Managers $166,790 (59% more) and Compensation and Benefits Managers $149,230 (42% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. These roles usually expect management experience.

faq.q: Do financial advisors need another degree to switch?
faq.a: Usually not. 23 of the 25 matches need no more education than financial advisors already have, and 2 usually need a graduate degree, including investment fund management. A bachelor's degree is common, held by 56% of workers in the closest match.

faq.q: What skills should financial advisors build?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are managing people, coordination, managing materials and time management. Judgment already rates 3.62 out of 5 for advisors in O*NET, so leading teams and running operations are the main steps toward finance management.
